n: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Paediatrics

faq.a: CRRT provides slow, continuous fluid removal, avoiding rapid haemodynamic shifts that can worsen shock and cerebral oedema.
faq.q: Why is CRRT preferred over intermittent HD in septic children?

faq.a: Citrate is preferred because it chelates calcium locally, reducing systemic anticoagulation and bleeding risk.
faq.q: What anticoagulant is safest in children with bleeding risk?

faq.a: Increase dialysate potassium concentration, adjust ultrafiltration, and give calcium gluconate if cardiac arrhythmias develop.
faq.q: How do you manage hyperkalaemia during CRRT?

exam: What is the first step in managing a child with AKI and hypotension requiring CRRT? — Identify and treat the underlying sepsis, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and begin fluid resuscitation before CRRT initiation.
Which laboratory value is most reliable to confirm AKI in a resource‑limited setting? — Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 12–24 h.
Why is citrate anticoagulation preferred over heparin in children with a high bleeding risk? — Citrate chelates calcium locally, reducing systemic anticoagulation and bleeding complications.
What complication is most likely if the ultrafiltration rate is increased too quickly? — Hypotension and cerebral oedema due to rapid fluid removal.

How would you differentiate CRRT from intermittent HD in a septic child? — CRRT is continuous, low‑dose, and used in haemodynamically unstable patients; intermittent HD is intermittent and higher dose.
What is the key monitoring parameter to avoid hypocalcaemia during CRRT? — Ionised calcium levels, with calcium gluconate supplementation as needed.
ai.title: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: CRRT is a low‑dose, continuous dialysis used in children with acute kidney injury who are haemodynamically unstable or septic. It replaces fluids and toxins slowly, avoiding rapid shifts that can worsen shock or cerebral oedema.

b: Unstable blood pressure or need for inotropes
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2) or hyperkalaemia >6.5 mEq/L
sections.p: CRRT is a continuous, low‑dose haemodialysis or haemofiltration that removes waste, fluid and electrolytes over 24 hours. Diagnosis is based on the KDIGO criteria for acute kidney injury (AKI) plus haemodynamic instability or severe sepsis.

b: Stage 2: Cr 2–3× baseline or urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 h
Stage 3: Cr >3× baseline or urine <0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 h or anuria >12 h
sections.p: KDIGO stages 2–3 define the need for CRRT. Stage 3 with oliguria/anuria, rising creatinine, or fluid overload >10% of body weight is most common indication.

In East Africa, the leading causes of AKI requiring CRRT are sepsis (especially malaria, typhoid, bacterial meningitis), volume depletion from diarrhoea, and nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs).

b: Fluid overload: peripheral oedema, ascites, pulmonary crackles
sections.p: Children appear fluid overloaded, tachycardic, hypotensive, with oliguria or anuria, and may have metabolic acidosis or hyperkalaemia. Neurologic signs include seizures or altered consciousness if cerebral oedema is present.

t.b: Baseline renal function; rising levels indicate AKI severity
Assess acidosis and guide bicarbonate therapy

b: Bleeding: monitor haemoglobin, platelets, clotting times
Catheter sepsis: look for erythema, fever, positive cultures
sections.p: CRRT can cause bleeding (due to heparin), hypotension, hypocalcaemia, and catheter-related sepsis. Monitor for sudden drops in blood pressure, new murmurs, or fever.

b: Antibiotics per local guidelines (e.g., ceftriaxone for typhoid)
Rehydration with isotonic fluids before CRRT
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis, rehydration for dehydration). CRRT settings: dose 20–25 mL/kg/h, low‑dose anticoagulation, continuous ultrafiltration. Supportive care includes blood pressure support, electrolyte correction, and infection control.
After CRRT, monitor renal function, electrolytes, and fluid balance. Prevention focuses on early recognition of sepsis, judicious use of nephrotoxins, and prompt rehydration of diarrhoea.
Acute tubular necrosis without haemodynamic instability (treated with intermittent HD) and fluid overload from heart failure (treated with diuretics).

b: Early AKI: Cr may be normal, but oliguria is key
Coagulation: aPTT may be normal if heparin is subtherapeutic
sections.p: Serum creatinine may be normal early in AKI; urine output is a more sensitive early marker. Coagulation tests can be falsely normal if heparin is not monitored closely.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in blood pressure despite inotropes
